lesson_title: The Grip That Decides Every Boiling Point
hook_text: Pentane and butan-1-ol weigh almost the same. One boils at 36 degrees. The other past 117. Why?
clip_script: Two molecules, nearly identical in mass. Pentane boils at 36,1 degrees — barely warmer than a summer day. Butan-1-ol, practically the same size, holds out until 117,7. What is going on? Every molecule wears velcro — weak little London forces that everything owns. Longer molecule, longer strip, more grip: that is why boiling points climb steadily up the alkane family, from ethane way down at minus 88 to decane at 174. Crumple the molecule with branches and the strips can't lie flat against each other — grip drops, boiling point drops. But some molecules carry upgrades. Aldehydes and ketones snap together with fridge magnets — a permanently positive end clicking onto a permanently negative one. And alcohols? Alcohols shake hands. A hydrogen bonded straight onto an oxygen grabs the oxygen of the next molecule — the hydrogen bond, the strongest grip in the topic. That handshake is the entire gap between pentane's 36 and butan-1-ol's 117. Carboxylic acids shake with BOTH hands and top every chart at once. So when your nail polish remover empties its own bottle overnight, you already know the secret: weak grip, easy escape, high vapour pressure. Strong grip, high boiling point. One idea — the whole topic.
visual_style: Molecules as characters wearing velcro strips pressing flat against each other, then crumpling into balls that barely touch; upgrade icons snapping on — a fridge magnet, two clasping hands — beside a thermometer climbing rung by rung.
mood: Curious and tactile — invisible forces made touchable.
pacing: Puzzle opening with the two thermometers, three quick upgrade beats, satisfying single-idea close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain any boiling point in four clean sentences.
